name: Aisha Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Aisha, 27, and I lead three operators working a cutting machine underground at a large mine. My two-year technical diploma helps me understand the machine, but the best part is feeling the cutter settle into a difficult seam without forcing it. I'm paid towards the lower end for this work, and a dental bill has left about eighteen days of expenses saved. I sometimes use AI to explain a manual's wording at home, then check the original; I don't want the mine's private information going into a chat box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a reliable cutter still matters more than any announcement about whether AI is changing everything or nothing. I don't mind a tool explaining a manual, provided the original instructions decide what we actually do with the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine still needs my crew, but eighteen days of savings doesn't feel like enough after the last dental bill. I know this work well; I still worry about losing paid shifts through illness before the rent leaves my account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the cutting crew and check the cutter teeth and emergency stop at the start of each shift. I'd delay buying a new sofa and transfer twenty each payday into the emergency account after paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about another bill, not about a software programme taking the controls in this picture. I keep thinking a person ought to feel more secure after becoming good at a difficult job, then I open the banking app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened after paying the dentist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I counted what was left against the rent and stopped looking at furniture adverts. Nothing dramatic happened at work that week, but I was doing sums while waiting for the lift underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you like enough to stay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the crew makes a clean cut through awkward ground, everybody knows we did the preparation right. I like going home tired for a reason, rather than wondering what my working day was for.

say: I'd say a **reliable cutter** still matters more than any announcement about whether AI is changing everything or nothing.
I don't mind a tool explaining a manual, provided the **original instructions** decide what we actually do with the machine.
think: The mine still needs my crew, but **eighteen days of savings** doesn't feel like enough after the last dental bill.
I know this work well; I still worry about **losing paid shifts** through illness before the rent leaves my account.
do: Keep leading the **cutting crew** and check the cutter teeth and emergency stop at the start of each shift.
Delay buying a **new sofa** and transfer twenty each payday into the emergency account after paying rent.
feel: **Anxious about interrupted pay**, while expecting the cutting work itself to stay much the same.
S0.quote: The mine still needs my crew, but eighteen days of savings doesn't feel like enough after the last dental bill.
fieldNote: Her **baseline anxiety** concerns interrupted wages and depleted savings, rather than assuming the plateau card introduces major new physical automation.
The **sofa delay** is a concrete household trade; pride in skilled work does not remove her need for a small emergency reserve.

steps.text: Lead cutting shifts and inspect cutter teeth and the emergency stop
Delay the sofa purchase and save twenty each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our crew better planning might help, but the cutter still has to get through the rock in front of us. I'd ask for a supervised trial before anyone turns an AI schedule into a target used against the operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my work is physical, so I expect to keep earning while planning staff face the earlier changes. My reserve is still small, and mistakes during a change could cost shifts even if the machine still needs a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd attend the dispatch trial beside an experienced operator and compare its cutting sequence with the actual ground on two shifts. I'd keep the sofa money untouched and continue twenty-per-payday transfers during the first year of the planning change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm interested if the trial is honest about mistakes, and anxious because I still can't absorb much lost pay. I don't expect my job to vanish now; I want learning time treated as work rather than a reason to dock a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would persuade you that the trial worked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let us compare the planned order with where the cutter actually slows down, then correct the next plan together. I wouldn't judge it from one perfect demonstration with no awkward ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join a campaign against the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just because it was software. I'd first ask what happened to errors, pay and training time, because those answers matter more to me than picking a side in a row.

say: I'd tell our crew **better planning** might help, but the cutter still has to get through the rock in front of us.
I'd ask for a **supervised trial** before anyone turns an AI schedule into a target used against the operators.
think: Most of my work is physical, so I expect to keep earning while **planning staff** face the earlier changes.
My reserve is still small, and **mistakes during a change** could cost shifts even if the machine still needs a person.
do: Attend the **dispatch trial** beside an experienced operator and compare its cutting sequence with the actual ground on two shifts.
Keep the **sofa money** untouched and continue twenty-per-payday transfers during the first year of the planning change.
feel: **Anxious about earnings**, with cautious interest in a system she can inspect before using alone.
S1.quote: I'd ask for a supervised trial before anyone turns an AI schedule into a target used against the operators.
fieldNote: Her **conditional acceptance** fits occasional AI use and a preference for evidence, with the trial tied to two concrete working shifts.
She expects **physical work** to persist, while thin savings preserve baseline anxiety and make fair treatment of learning errors especially important.

steps.text: Compare the dispatch trial with actual cutting conditions on two shifts
Keep the sofa money untouched and continue payday emergency transfers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2028 thinking AI could change the plans before robot cutters arrive around 2031, so we need two preparation dates. I'd ask the mine for a paid equipment course, with proper hours rather than homework added after an underground shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a smaller operator crew when robots can cut, and I don't have enough money for a long job search. The first two years might still bring paid shifts, but rent after a cut is what keeps coming back at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid equipment-testing course this quarter and check whether former trainees actually got work before applying. I'd cancel the cinema membership now and save the fee through 2029 in case planning changes reduce the available shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed because I can see the mine needing fewer operators and I don't know whether I'd be kept. I keep waking to think about an empty pay date, even while I can list sensible questions to ask tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why testing rather than another office job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The equipment is something I understand, so finding faults would build on that knowledge. I know testing can also change with AI; I'd ask what the actual work is before treating the course as a rescue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first year after 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking cutting shifts while they existed and check whether the course led to paid practical work. The extra three years before robots would help only if I used them, but I couldn't simply stop earning to study.

say: I'd say **2028 thinking AI** could change the plans before robot cutters arrive around 2031, so we need two preparation dates.
I'd ask the mine for a **paid equipment course**, with proper hours rather than homework added after an underground shift.
think: I expect a **smaller operator crew** when robots can cut, and I don't have enough money for a long job search.
The first two years might still bring paid shifts, but **rent after a cut** is what keeps coming back at night.
do: Ask for a **paid equipment-testing course** this quarter and check whether former trainees actually got work before applying.
Cancel the **cinema membership** now and save the fee through 2029 in case planning changes reduce the available shifts.
feel: **Alarmed about losing pay**, with a possible learning route that still needs a place and funding.
S2.quote: I'd ask the mine for a paid equipment course, with proper hours rather than homework added after an underground shift.
fieldNote: She anticipates **operator losses** and reports disturbed sleep, supporting alarm even though the physical replacement date follows thinking AI by three years.
Her **training request** builds on existing equipment knowledge but remains conditional on funding and employment evidence, without promising immunity from automation.

steps.text: Request paid equipment-testing training and check former trainees’ employment
Cancel the cinema membership and retain the fee through 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us check which courses actually help before the mine's planning changes in 2031. We should prepare while cutting shifts still pay, rather than wait until robot equipment reaches the mine around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could save in small amounts and take a short course without losing wages; five years makes that believable. The job could still disappear, and few nearby mines means I shouldn't assume another operator wage will be waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take one evening equipment-testing module after a practical taster, without signing up for a costly full course immediately. I'd increase emergency transfers to twenty-five each payday and review the balance during the first year after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about losing the role, and the present dental-sized bill would still hurt. Five years makes the planning feel manageable because I can try one module and see how much energy I actually have after work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop after one module?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If all the teaching was about software buttons and none of it involved equipment, I'd ask whether it matched any actual job. I wouldn't keep paying just because I'd already bought the first section.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes when 2031 arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the new mine organisation with the equipment jobs being advertised and keep learning only where there was a use for it. I would still have roughly three years before the robot date, not three years to stop paying attention.

say: I'd say **five years** lets us check which courses actually help before the mine's planning changes in 2031.
We should prepare while **cutting shifts** still pay, rather than wait until robot equipment reaches the mine around 2034.
think: I could save in small amounts and take a short course without losing wages; **five years** makes that believable.
The job could still disappear, and **few nearby mines** means I shouldn't assume another operator wage will be waiting.
do: Take one **evening equipment-testing module** after a practical taster, without signing up for a costly full course immediately.
Increase emergency transfers to **twenty-five each payday** and review the balance during the first year after 2031.
feel: **Anxious but organised**, with time to test study alongside paid work rather than make one large bet.
S3.quote: We should prepare while cutting shifts still pay, rather than wait until robot equipment reaches the mine around 2034.
fieldNote: The **longer warning** changes the scale of her decision from an urgent funded place to a small study trial alongside wages.
Persistent **financial anxiety** and limited nearby employment prevent the practical plan from becoming a claim that enough warning guarantees another job.

steps.text: Try one evening equipment-testing module after a practical taster
Save twenty-five each payday and review the balance after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues a decade gives us room to try another skill, but we still need wages while we learn. By 2036 planning could be very different, and robot cutters around 2039 would arrive while I'm still young enough to need work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can plan a route in stages rather than rush, but training promises still need to match jobs somebody actually pays for. Ten years doesn't change the eighteen-day reserve I have now, so I need a small financial plan as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd arrange a practical course visit on a day off this year and ask two working technicians what the training really covers. I'd review the emergency account every quarter, keeping that habit through 2037 rather than assuming the distant robot date solves current bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm less frightened of the date, but still anxious about the next unexpected bill. Having ten years means I can ask awkward questions before spending money, which feels useful even if nobody can promise a safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the technicians?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what they actually do all day and how often their employers take beginners. Then I'd ask how the work itself might change, because moving into another exposed job without knowing would be a nasty surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do during 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep earning on the cutter if the shifts remained, review the account and compare course progress with real vacancies. The thinking AI would already be here in this picture, so I'd judge the plan against what had happened rather than the brochure from ten years earlier.

say: I'd tell colleagues **a decade** gives us room to try another skill, but we still need wages while we learn.
By 2036 planning could be very different, and **robot cutters around 2039** would arrive while I'm still young enough to need work.
think: I can plan a route in stages rather than rush, but **training promises** still need to match jobs somebody actually pays for.
Ten years doesn't change the **eighteen-day reserve** I have now, so I need a small financial plan as well.
do: Arrange a **practical course visit** on a day off this year and ask two working technicians what the training really covers.
Review the **emergency account every quarter**, keeping that habit through 2037 rather than assuming the distant robot date solves current bills.
feel: **Anxious about current money**, while the distant work change feels less urgent and easier to investigate.
S4.quote: Ten years doesn't change the eighteen-day reserve I have now, so I need a small financial plan as well.
fieldNote: She uses **a decade** for staged investigation rather than retirement, and keeps the distinction between 2036 thinking AI and 2039 physical automation.
Her **current reserve** remains central across scenarios; distant employment change lowers urgency without erasing the household risk she brought into the interview.

steps.text: Visit a practical course and ask two technicians about real work
Review emergency savings quarterly and retain that review through 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest because I expect fewer paid operators around 2031 and can't yet afford a gap between wages. A paid course tied to real equipment work and a clear decision date would help more than being told to stay positive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the time between being accepted for training and actually being paid. My cutting machine gives a warning before trouble; my bank balance usually tells me too late.

headlineQuote: My cutting machine gives a warning before trouble; my bank balance usually tells me too late.
portrait: A **27-year-old cutting-machine leader**, she values careful listening underground and uses her technical diploma to understand why equipment behaves differently.
A **dental bill** has reduced her reserve to eighteen days of expenses, making steady but low-paid work financially fragile.
She uses **AI occasionally**, checks explanations against manuals and wants practical demonstrations before spending money or trusting a new work system.
Longer warning allows **gradual preparation**, but she measures possible courses against paid hours, actual vacancies and the dates wages might stop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could leave her without operator wages before she can fund a reliable move into different work.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid equipment training** with clear dates and real employment links would help her prepare without losing the income covering current bills.
